historical_claims.anchor: As Davis and Kahan emphasize, no separate hypothesis excludes the angles where the tangent of two theta is infinite, at forty-five degrees, and no spectral hypothesis is placed on the perturbed blocks.
That is how the paper uses the theorem for the free beam.

Davis and Kahan state that all four constants are best possible, attained in two dimensions, and that for a perturbation depending linearly on a small parameter the four estimates agree to first order.
Davis and Kahan record that, unlike the doubled-sine theorem, no extension of the doubled-tangent theorem to a trial subspace of smaller dimension than the exact one was known to them.
This is the rotation used in Jacobi's classical method for symmetric eigenvalue problems, which annihilates one off-diagonal entry at a time.
